extracted.intended_audience: readers of classic literature and writers interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of an 18th‑century novel excerpt (Tristram Shandy) that includes authorial commentary on narrative technique (digressions, character-drawing, audience/critics). Useful for studying digressive narrative and satirical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digressions are essential (value of digression)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Digressions, incontestably, are the sunshine;——they are the life, the soul of reading!—take them out of this book, for instance,—you might as well take the book along with them;—one cold eternal winter would reign in every page of it; restore them to the writer;—he steps forth like a bridegroom,—bids All-hail; brings in variety, and forbids the appetite to fail.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial claim that digressions are central to engaging reading; they provide variety and keep appetite alive. The passage treats digressions positively and as a core design choice for a lively book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage digressions so the main narrative continues
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the dexterity is in the good cookery and management of them, so as to be not only for the advantage of the reader, but also of the author, whose distress, in this matter, is truly pitiable: For, if he begins a digression,—from that moment, I observe, his whole work stands stock still;—and if he goes on with his main work,—then there is an end of his digression.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical prescription: organize the work so digressive and progressive movements are interwoven ("one wheel within another") to prevent the main business from halting. The author illustrates structural techniques: construct main and adventitious parts with intersections so the 'machine' is kept a-going.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw character without mechanical or one-dimensional aids
rubrics_metrics.description: “To avoid all and every one of these errors in giving you my uncle Toby’s character, I am determined to draw it by no mechanical help whatever;—nor shall my pencil be guided by any one wind-instrument which ever was blown upon...nor will I consider either his repletions or his discharges,—or touch upon his Non-naturals; but, in a word, I will draw my uncle Toby’s character from his HOBBY-HORSE.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive anti-patterns to avoid when depicting character: do not rely solely on musical metaphors (wind-instruments), bodily evacuations, mechanical copying (pentagraph), photographic/'camera' views, or caricatured lighting ('against the light'). Instead, base character on a distinctive, revealing personal trait or obsession (the 'hobby-horse') and use that as the organizing principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting readers anticipate upcoming events
rubrics_metrics.description: “in this, Sir, I am of so nice and singular a humour, that if I thought you was able to form the least judgment or probable conjecture to yourself, of what was to come in the next page,—I would tear it out of my book.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial advice to preserve unpredictability: do not telegraph the next page or upcoming developments; keep the reader unaware to maintain interest and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include and court critics rather than exclude them
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is nothing so foolish, when you are at the expence of making an entertainment of this kind, as to order things so badly, as to let your criticks and gentry of refined taste run it down: Nor is there any thing so likely to make them do it, as that of leaving them out of the party... I have left half a dozen places purposely open for them;—and in the next place, I pay them all court.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance about audience management: include critics deliberately, give them visible places, and treat them courteously ("pay them court") to avoid antagonizing them and to reduce negative reception.
